opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a lot of room there. The core idea we were going after is that when a model sees a particular document, some of what it learns is general, shared knowledge, and some is idiosyncratic, specific to that document. If you let both get tangled up in the same parameters, it becomes very hard to remove the specific stuff later without hurting the general capabilities. So the intuition was: give each document, or each sequence, some dedicated set of neurons where its idiosyncratic content can "sink," and keep the shared neurons for things that generalize.

Where I see room to improve is in a few places. The first is how the assignment happens. Right now it's fairly simple. You use something like a hash of the document's identity to decide which neurons get activated for it. That's nice because it's cheap and deterministic, but it doesn't use anything about the content. You could imagine a smarter scheme where documents that are near-duplicates, or share a lot of rare content, get routed in more coordinated ways, because duplication is a big driver of memorization in the first place.

The second is scale and capacity. As you go to really large pretraining corpora, you can't give every document a truly unique set of neurons, so there's overlap and collisions. Understanding how much capacity you need to reserve, and how that trades off against the general-purpose part of the model, is still pretty open. We had some empirical evidence it works at the scales we tried, but I'd want a more principled understanding of how it extrapolates.

Third, there's the question of what counts as a unit. We worked at the level of documents or sequences, but memorization isn't always neatly aligned with document boundaries. Sometimes the thing you'd want to isolate is a specific fact, a person's name, or a piece of code that appears across many documents. So thinking about finer-grained or more semantic units for isolation would be really interesting.

And finally, I'd love to see this connected more tightly to downstream goals like unlearning, privacy, and copyright. The promise is that if memorized content lives in known places, you can just drop or zero out those neurons when you need to. Actually stress-testing that, with strong extraction attacks and realistic unlearning requests, is where I think the next round of work needs to go. It's one thing to show memorization is reduced on average; it's another to give guarantees people can rely on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few places where I'd be honest about the limitations. The core idea is that when you're trying to get a model to memorize specific documents, or really to isolate the influence of specific documents, you carve out dedicated subspaces of neurons so that the knowledge from each document lives somewhere you can find it and, if you need to, remove it. That part works surprisingly well. But the way we assign those subspaces right now is pretty rigid.

The first issue is granularity. We're treating a document as the unit, and documents are not a natural unit of knowledge. A single Wikipedia article contains dozens of facts that may be shared with hundreds of other documents, and a long book might really be a collection of fairly independent pieces. So when you assign one document to one subspace, you're imposing a partition on the knowledge that doesn't match how the information actually overlaps. I'd love to see a version where the assignment is driven by something more semantic, where documents that share a lot of content end up sharing parameters, and the subspace structure reflects the dependency structure in the data rather than just the file boundaries.

The second thing is scale. With a modest number of documents you can afford to give each one its own slice. As you go to pretraining-scale corpora, the subspaces have to get very small or you have to share them heavily, and at that point you lose some of the clean attribution guarantees that made the approach appealing in the first place. There's an interesting question about whether you can do something hierarchical, where you have coarse groups of documents with shared capacity and then finer-grained allocations within them. I don't think we've found the right design there yet.

And then the third piece, which I think is maybe the most important, is that we're intervening at the level of parameters, but what we actually care about is behavior. If you ablate a document's subspace and the model stops reproducing that document, that's good, but it doesn't tell you whether the model has picked up the same information through some other path, through generalization from the rest of the corpus. So we need better evaluations of whether the isolation is real in a functional sense, not just a structural sense. That connects to a lot of the unlearning literature, where it's very easy to fool yourself into thinking you've removed something when you've really just made it harder to elicit.

So I'd say the paper is a proof of concept that you can shape where knowledge lands during training, and the open work is making the assignment smarter, making it scale, and making sure the guarantees we think we have actually hold up under adversarial probing.

astra-6.text:
I think one direction is making the assignment more flexible. Giving each document its own neuron subspace gives us a clear way to separate information, but documents aren’t really independent. They can overlap or contain complementary pieces of information. So how do we allow useful sharing while preserving the ability to isolate what came from a particular document?

There’s also the question of how much capacity each document needs. A fixed allocation might be too much for some documents and too little for others. Learning that allocation, and understanding how it scales as we add documents, would be interesting directions to explore.

That’s an interesting tradeoff between efficiency, model quality, and how much control the structure gives us.
